pr_title: Stop trying to estimate IL sizes
pr_body:
- We originally did this to reduce the amount of resizes when generating IL for huge method bodies but now that we don't inline the transitive closure of scoped dependencies, we can just estimate a modest size that avoids *most* resizes (512).
- The current ILEmitCallsiteAnalyzer doesn't keep track of visited callsites so can over estimate the size. Instread of fixing it, just delete it.

Fixes https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/36374

cc @brandondahler

issue_context.title: ASP.NET Core Dependency Injection container uses excessive amount of memory and CPU when large dependency graph is created
issue_context.body:
### Description
ASP.NET Core Dependency Injection container uses excessive amount of memory and CPU when large dependency graph is created.

### How To Reproduce
I created a [repository](https://github.com/sergey-kolodiy/AspNetCore.DI) with a small project that reproduces the issue. It targets .NET Framework 4.7.2, but the issue is also reproducible for .NET Core 2.2.

1. Build the solution and run `AspNetCore.DI.Default` project.
2. Using Fiddler or some other tool of your choice, send multiple simultaneous HTTP requests to `http://localhost:5000/api/values` API endpoint. The issue is not always reproduced if you send a single HTTP request and then just wait for the response.
3. Observe resources consumption. You should see significant increase in both CPU and memory consumption:
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/741576/64855546-cabe0f00-d628-11e9-8523-01e74f913e48.png)
4. For comparison, run `AspNetCore.DI.Autofac` project that uses Autofac DI container instead of the default one and send multiple HTTP API requests again. You won't see those CPU and memory peaks this time.

### Expected behavior
Obviously the default DI container shouldn't use that much CPU and memory resources.

### So, what's going on?
Web API from the example above uses MVC middleware only, but, in addition to MVC services, it also registers a bunch of services with `Scoped` lifetime that are organized in a large graph (without any circular dependencies), and it seems like the default ASP.NET Core DI container is having some issues handling it.

In the request processing thread, the dependency graph is created and injected into the `ValuesController` just fine, and the API returns HTTP 200. But, it looks like for every dependency graph encountered, default DI container (or ASP.NET Core runtime) also spawns a separate background thread that performs some sort of initial processing and/or caching of that dependency graph. So, in theory this operation shouldn't affect request processing threads (at least when the dependency graph is relatively small).

However, it seems like this graph processing algorithm complexity grows exponentially, so the bigger dependency graph is, the more time and memory is consumed by this background operation. On my machine I had peaks up to 100% CPU (completely freezed) and more that 11GB memory consumption, which is not acceptable for production.

After this background process is done, resource consumption slowly decreases back to normal, and it doesn't start again when I invoke API methods on that controller, but for other controllers with different dependency graphs it starts again.

This issue is not reproducible when using Autofac DI container.
comments: This should be fixed/improved in 3.0. I'll try out the project.

TL;DR The issue is fixed in 3.0.

**UPDATE:** I hit another issue in development mode where the recursive walk ends up being O(N!). This only seems to be slow in development. Running it in production to see if I can see the memory issue.

As a workaround, if you turn off scope validation, it should be fast:

```C#
public static IWebHostBuilder CreateWebHostBuilder(string[] args) =>
            WebHost.CreateDefaultBuilder(args)
                .UseStartup<Startup>()
                .UseDefaultServiceProvider(o => o.ValidateScopes = false);
```

**UPDATE:** Finally got a repro:

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/95136/64903891-29f64080-d676-11e9-80e2-7c11c416920c.png)

**UPDATE:** The issue is fixed with the latest preview version of Microsoft.DependencyInjection.Extensions.

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/95136/64903915-7c376180-d676-11e9-9f55-d4cf29f8d09c.png)

Seems like memory issue is fixed in the latest `Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection` preview, but CPU is still increasing from 0 to ~17% on my machine and not dropping, even with `ValidateScopes = false` flag, for both .NET Core 2.2 and 3.0 preview (SDK 3.0.100-preview9-014004).

After doing some performance debugging, I found that ILEmitCallSiteAnalyzer is O(n!).  See branch at https://github.com/brandondahler/Extensions/tree/bugfix/DI/LargeGraphExcessiveCPU_InitialTest   for a test that shows/exercises this worst-case scenario -- test name "ResolveService_LargeGraph".

~Caching should possible, similar to how dotnet/extensions#2374 was done, to reduce the time complexity to O(n).  Will likely provide PR for this issue soon.~

Edit: Wrong, see comment below.

From what I can tell, ILEmitCallSiteAnalyzer's only purpose is to make a good estimate for ILEmitResolverBuilder's `dynamicMethod.GetILGenerator(info.Size);` call; however, it looks like we updated the way that we're generating the IL in ILEmitResolverBuilder at https://github.com/aspnet/Extensions/commit/1424884389d95c89687229431f79d280bac61495; however, we didn't subsequently update the logic in ILEmitCallSiteAnalyzer.

In particular, it appears that we are generating significantly smaller amounts of IL by calling the ResolveService dynamic methods per-service (technically per-service-slot) instead of presumably nesting these resolution.  Long story short, I believe that something like dotnet/extensions#2375 might be the correct fix for it, but clarity and/or validation from @pakrym or other aspnet members would be needed to proceed further.

I wonder if we can remove ILEmitCallSiteAnalyzer all together, we aren't going to generate massive trees like before with scoped services being separate so maybe this optimization doesn't matter.

We can also try to update ILGenerator in corefx to use array pool

100% agree @pakrym on removing ILEmitCallSiteAnalyzer.  I think defaulting to 1024 or 2048 would be sufficient to cover normal cases without grossly over-allocating.  If I can get alignment on this direction, I'll update my PR accordingly.

### Details
Doing a quick analysis on the size of the generated IL of different maximally dense trees, I found they follow these approximate sizes:
* Transient - 5 * 2^n
* Scoped - 90 + 22n
* Singleton - 16n

While the IL generated being is O(2^n) in size, this presumably isn't that big of an issue because the total number of constructed objects in this case would also be O(2^x), meaning that the size of the IL generated is linearly related to the total number of objects to be constructed.

If I'm expanding this logic right, 1024 bytes should be enough IL space for us to construct ~200 transient object instances, ~50 scoped object instances, or ~64 singleton object instances.

review_comments:
> but we could potentially change ILGenerator to use the array pool

I'm skeptical we would do this.
https://github.com/dotnet/designs/blob/main/accepted/2021/runtime-security-mitigations.md#protect-intermediate-language-il-code
It introduces potential issues where an array is erronously returned to the pool while still in use, then the ILGenerator picks up that array and uses it to write IL, and now whoever returned the array to the pool is potentially able to write IL that'll be executed.

Sure, I don't think it matters anymore really. We don't generate large methods anymore anyways 😄. Also now that we have this event, we can ask people to turn it on and see what sizes we get in practice to adjust this number.
Is it worth moving this magic number out into a const and adding a further remark of why 512 was chosen?
I would normally agree if it used in more than on place. I could add size: 512 to make it a bit clearer but the comment is inline.
